title: Can we create a new example?
learning_goal: What was the system given?
visual_description: Application 1: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: Give students ten seconds to inspect faces, rooms and animals. These are published samples, not photographs. Ask what inputs each task might require. Our question is how learning to remove noise can define a generator.
question: What was the system given?
answer: Unconditional generation needs a random starting state; conditional tasks also receive information such as text or observed pixels.
talk_through: Look at the variety here. What would a model need to learn to make another example?
takeaway: A generator learns from examples so that it can produce new samples.
explanation_steps: What would we need to create another example?
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: One description, several valid images
learning_goal: Which sample is the correct target?
visual_description: Application 2: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: Read the source prompt above the column, then reveal the diversity question. These are different published samples, not a documented fixed-seed experiment. Hold this prompt and sample identity fixed when returning to text conditioning.
question: Which sample is the correct target?
answer: There need not be one unique correct image; the target is a conditional distribution.
talk_through: We have one prompt. Before seeing the other samples, would you expect one correct image?
takeaway: The prompt describes a distribution of possible images, so different samples can all fit.
explanation_steps: “A basket full of cherries”
Several different images can fit the same description.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Where should the objects go?
learning_goal: Do boxes determine every pixel?
visual_description: Application 3: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: Point to the boxes before discussing output images. The project supplies grounding layouts and captions. Do not claim matched seeds or perfect compositional adherence. Later we distinguish spatial conditions from text features.
question: Do boxes determine every pixel?
answer: No. They constrain location while appearance remains uncertain.
talk_through: The boxes tell us where objects belong. Which choices are still left to the model?
takeaway: A layout constrains object positions while leaving room for different appearances.
explanation_steps: A condition can specify where objects should appear.
The layout still leaves choices about appearance.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Fill a missing region
learning_goal: Must a plausible completion recover the original?
visual_description: Application 4: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: Use the first row from the same RePaint comparison. The final five columns are distinct samples, not successive timesteps; the middle columns of the original are denoising states. Return to this exact face in Scene 54.
question: Must a plausible completion recover the original?
answer: No. It samples a possible explanation, not necessarily the image that was hidden.
talk_through: We can see part of this face. What would count as a plausible way to fill the blue region?
takeaway: The visible pixels constrain the answer, but several completions can still make sense.
explanation_steps: We observe part of the face; the blue region is missing.
Several plausible faces can match those visible pixels.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Turn rough strokes into a plausible image
learning_goal: What changes with stronger initial noise?
visual_description: Application 5: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: SDEdit corrupts an input and uses a learned denoising process. The model is not trained anew for every sketch, and preserving every supplied pixel is not its promise. Invite predictions before revealing the output rows.
question: What changes with stronger initial noise?
answer: The input can exert less influence; a plausible image need not preserve exact strokes.
talk_through: These strokes suggest colours and a layout. How closely should the result follow them?
takeaway: More initial noise gives the model more freedom and can weaken the influence of the strokes.
explanation_steps: Start from rough colour strokes.
The starting noise level controls how strongly the strokes guide the result.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: What detail is missing at low resolution?
learning_goal: Does a realistic eyelash establish that it was observed?
visual_description: Application 6: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: Keep the source labels. This asset supplies an actual paired reference. Bicubic is an interpolation baseline; regression and diffusion differ in how they represent missing detail. Avoid claiming that realism verifies what was measured.
question: Does a realistic eyelash establish that it was observed?
answer: No; evaluate against held-out references and the observation model.
talk_through: Zooming in cannot tell us which fine details were really there. What can the model add?
takeaway: Generated detail may look convincing without recovering the detail in the original scene.
explanation_steps: The low-resolution image leaves fine detail uncertain.
A realistic detail is one possible explanation of the observation.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Draw the structure, generate the appearance
learning_goal: Which part is the condition?
visual_description: Application 7: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: Identify the edge map explicitly. A control module gives one way to inject spatial conditions; it is not part of every diffusion model. The scene makes a connection to dense vision before introducing a new backbone.
question: Which part is the condition?
answer: The edge map; the colourful image is a generated output.
talk_through: We used edge maps to describe images. Here we use one to guide the creation of an image.
takeaway: Spatial features can serve as conditions that guide where image structure appears.
explanation_steps: An edge map records the structure of an image.
We can use that structure to guide a generated image.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Put a particular subject in a new context
learning_goal: When do the reference images enter?
visual_description: Application 8: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: The references are used during subject-specific adaptation. Do not draw them as an unchanged model input at each inference step. Ask which identity features remain recognisable when the context changes.
question: When do the reference images enter?
answer: During adaptation; prompts condition the adapted model during generation.
talk_through: The reference images teach the model about this subject before we ask for a new setting.
takeaway: DreamBooth adapts a model to a subject; prompts then guide images made by that adapted model.
explanation_steps: Use reference images to adapt the model to this subject.
Then ask for the subject in a new setting.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Could this help answer a lab question?
learning_goal: What would establish scientific usefulness?
visual_description: Application 9: source evidence with explicit condition and generated outputs.
narration: The left evidence is a published DiffusionSat result. The small diagram is a possible lab research task, not an accomplished lab result. Ask how measurement consistency, held-out tests and uncertainty would be assessed.
question: What would establish scientific usefulness?
answer: Validation against withheld measurements and an explicit observation model, beyond visual plausibility.
talk_through: For a scientific task, how would we check whether a plausible image agrees with the measurements?
takeaway: Scientific usefulness needs validation against observations, beyond a convincing image.
explanation_steps: Coordinates, metadata and observations can condition a model.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: What must a generator learn?
learning_goal: What three questions remain?
visual_description: Sampling loop: random noise, shared denoiser, reverse transition, feedback of sampled state.
narration: After concrete applications, introduce the abstraction. c is omitted for unconditional generation. We will first implement one historical DDPM formulation; gallery methods need not share every detail.
question: What three questions remain?
answer: How to create training examples, what to predict, and how to use the prediction to sample.
talk_through: All these examples involve sampling, sometimes with extra information that narrows the possibilities.
takeaway: We need a training example, a prediction target and a rule that turns predictions into samples.
explanation_steps: p_\theta(x\mid c)
How do we build training examples, choose a target and generate a sample?
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: From one-step generators to a denoising chain
learning_goal: Connect to Lecture I
visual_description: Compare a one-pass latent generator with repeated state updates by a shared diffusion denoiser.
narration: Reconnect to the actual course diagrams. A VAE has a prior and decoder, a GAN an induced distribution through a generator. Diffusion parameterises a different chain of transformations, not a universal improvement claim.
talk_through: A VAE or GAN maps a random latent to an image. How might we build that image through many steps?
takeaway: Diffusion generates through a chain of denoising steps that share one learned model.
explanation_steps: In Lecture I, we drew a latent and passed it through a generator.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: A digit gradually loses information
learning_goal: A digit gradually loses information
visual_description: The same digit under six stages of a recorded forward corruption chain.
narration: The random seed is 667; every transition draws new independent noise. The display clips to a fixed intensity range, but the arrays do not. Distinguish this joint trajectory from the direct marginal slider later.
talk_through: Follow the same digit across the row. Which features disappear first as we add noise?
takeaway: Repeated corruption gradually makes the original digit harder to identify.
explanation_steps: Follow the same MNIST test digit, index 0, across time.
Each transition adds a fresh, independent noise draw.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Can we recover the original with certainty?
learning_goal: Can removing noise be a unique inverse?
visual_description: Two illustrative corruption densities overlap at a possible observed coordinate.
narration: This is a schematic of overlapping support, not a claim that two independently sampled arrays are identical. The learned predictor uses the training distribution to estimate missing information.
question: Can removing noise be a unique inverse?
answer: Generally no. Corruption loses information; inference uses a distribution over explanations.
talk_through: If several clean images could have produced this observation, how could we pick the original with certainty?
takeaway: Denoising uses learned patterns to handle the uncertainty left by corruption.
explanation_steps: Two different digits can have overlapping noisy distributions.
The noisy observation may fit more than one clean image.
p(x_0\mid x_t)\ \text{can retain uncertainty}
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: What happens to a whole distribution?
learning_goal: Watch a distribution, not just a picture
narration: Use fixed axes. These particles represent the distribution, not eight uncertainty estimates for one image. The reverse recurrence uses the exact mixture score but a finite-step Gaussian approximation. Show the label throughout.
talk_through: Each dot is a sample. Watch how the whole collection changes as the noise level rises.
takeaway: Noise changes a distribution; this toy example lets us calculate its score analytically.
explanation_steps: Watch eight Gaussian clusters spread out as noise increases.
Here we can calculate the score exactly, without training a network.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: What is a clean image tensor?
learning_goal: What is \(x_0\)?
visual_description: A real digit, a schematic coordinate grid and the exact clean pixel normalisation.
narration: Pixels are not probabilities here. Our clean training values lie in [-1,1], but noisy tensors may leave it. Clip only display pixels. The scalar fixture is arithmetic, not the value of every digit pixel.
talk_through: Start with one pixel value, then imagine doing the same calculation at every position in the tensor.
takeaway: Our clean pixels lie in [−1, 1], but adding Gaussian noise can take values outside that range.
explanation_steps: An image is a tensor of real-valued coordinates.
x_0=1\quad\text{for one illustrative coordinate}
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: One small corruption step
learning_goal: What is chosen and what is random?
visual_description: A branched addition: scale current signal, add independent Gaussian noise, obtain the next state.
narration: Beta contributes variance; square root beta scales a standard Gaussian. Eta is independent per-step noise. We reserve epsilon for the aggregate noise in a marginal sample.
question: What is chosen and what is random?
answer: The schedule is chosen; eta is random. Given the previous state, the next state is sampled.
talk_through: We shrink the current signal slightly, then add a fresh Gaussian draw. Why are there square roots?
takeaway: Beta specifies the added variance, so the noise amplitude is the square root of beta.
explanation_steps: \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1}
\eta_t\sim\mathcal N(0,I)
x_t=\sqrt{1-\beta_t}x_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\eta_t
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Alpha and alpha-bar mean different things
learning_goal: Alpha and alpha-bar mean different things
visual_description: Two-step example: one-step alpha is 0.8; cumulative signal variance retention is 0.64.
narration: Keep the bar visible. One alpha describes one transition; their product describes cumulative signal variance retention. The two-step schedule is deliberately large for arithmetic.
talk_through: One alpha describes one step. What happens to the signal after we multiply several such steps?
takeaway: Alpha-bar is the product of the stepwise alphas and tracks cumulative signal variance retention.
explanation_steps: \alpha_t=1-\beta_t
\bar\alpha_2=\alpha_1\alpha_2=0.64
\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s,\quad\bar\alpha_0=1
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Jump directly to a training noise level
learning_goal: Why do variances add?
visual_description: Independent scaled noise terms combine by adding their variances.
narration: Substitute the first step into the second. Independence allows the two variances to add. The last line samples the correct marginal; sharing epsilon across times does not reproduce the joint Markov chain.
question: Why do variances add?
answer: The Gaussian noise terms are independent, so covariance cross terms vanish.
talk_through: Expand two steps first. The independent noise terms combine into one Gaussian with a known variance.
takeaway: We can sample a noisy training input at any chosen time without simulating all earlier steps.
explanation_steps: x_2=\sqrt{\alpha_2\alpha_1}x_0+\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}\eta_1+\sqrt{\beta_2}\eta_2
\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2=\alpha_2(1-\alpha_1)+(1-\alpha_2)=1-\alpha_1\alpha_2
q(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)I)
x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Work through one noisy coordinate
learning_goal: One forward calculation, fully worked
visual_description: Worked forward coordinate: 0.8 times one plus 0.6 times negative 0.5 equals 0.5.
narration: The arithmetic schedule beta1=beta2=.2 leaves 64% signal variance retention, so its endpoint is not noise-only. Do not reuse it to justify a standard Gaussian sampling start.
talk_through: Let us do the arithmetic for one coordinate: scale the clean value, scale the noise, then add.
takeaway: The signal and noise contributions can cancel; a noisy value alone does not identify either contribution.
explanation_steps: x_0=1,\quad\bar\alpha_2=.64,\quad\epsilon=-.5
\sqrt{.64}=.8,\quad\sqrt{1-.64}=.6
x_2=.5
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Try changing the noise level
learning_goal: Interact with the corruption
narration: Move the timestep and select a coordinate. The slider computes real arrays and coefficients. Reset restores seed 667 and inputs; resample changes the random array explicitly. The linear training endpoint is approximately 4.04e-5.
talk_through: Hold the seed fixed and move time. Then switch modes to see what changes when each step draws fresh noise.
takeaway: Direct sampling gives the correct distribution at each time; a recursive path also specifies how times relate.
explanation_steps: With fixed ε, the slider shares one noise array across times.
In recursive mode, every step draws fresh noise.
SNR = ᾱt / (1−ᾱt); at t=0 it is infinite.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Which target should the network predict?
learning_goal: Which target do we teach?
visual_description: Training branches: build the noisy input, predict its noise, and compare with the retained target.
narration: Select noise prediction as a parameterisation. All output entries are unconstrained real values. The architecture is a choice; the target is not a sigmoid probability map.
question: Which target do we teach?
answer: Aggregate Gaussian noise; alternative parameterisations remain possible.
talk_through: We could predict several quantities. In this lecture, we choose the Gaussian noise used to make the input.
takeaway: The denoiser takes a noisy image and its timestep, then predicts a real-valued noise tensor.
explanation_steps: Should we predict the clean image, the reverse mean or the added noise?
\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Assemble one training example
learning_goal: Assemble one training example
narration: Inspect the same coordinate across panels. The prediction panel replays actual predictions from the new compatible trained model for the selected digit, noise level and seed. The controls select cached tuples; they do not run or retrain a model in the browser. The noise target comes from exactly the displayed input construction.
talk_through: We made the noisy input ourselves, so we can keep the exact noise array as its training label.
takeaway: The model sees only the noisy image and time; the sampled noise stays on the target side.
explanation_steps: Draw a clean image, a timestep and a noise array.
Give the network only the noisy image and its time, (xt,t).
Compare the prediction with the noise ε we used.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Calculate the loss for four values
learning_goal: Compute a real loss value
visual_description: Illustrative two by two target and prediction tensors; squared errors sum to 0.15 and average to 0.0375.
narration: Four values form a 2 by 2 image. Sum of squared errors is .15; its mean is .0375. The training script averages over examples and all coordinates. These small predictions are illustrative activations.
talk_through: Compare each predicted value with its target, square the difference, and average over the four entries.
takeaway: Averaging over tensor entries turns the prediction errors into one scalar training loss.
explanation_steps: \operatorname{MSE}=\frac{.01+.04+.01+.09}{4}=.0375
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Can the network know the exact sampled noise?
learning_goal: Is the random seed an input?
visual_description: An illustrative conditional distribution with uncertainty; MSE predicts the conditional mean.
narration: The expectation is over clean examples and noise compatible with the observation. Under population squared error, the optimum is their conditional mean. This does not recover each hidden random draw exactly.
question: Is the random seed an input?
answer: No. A denoiser estimates using the observed noisy state and noise level.
talk_through: We know which noise we sampled. The model has less information: it sees only the noisy input and time.
takeaway: Under squared error, the best population prediction is the conditional mean of the possible noise values.
explanation_steps: We know the target noise. The model sees only (xt,t).
\epsilon_\theta^*(x_t,t)=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_t,t]
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: One denoiser, many noise levels
learning_goal: One denoiser, many noise levels
visual_description: Different timesteps enter one shared denoiser; time features condition its residual blocks.
narration: Time features recall positional encoding but represent corruption level, not sequence position. They let the same filters change their interpretation of an input. There are not 1,000 independent networks.
talk_through: The same input pattern can mean different things at low and high noise. We give the model time to distinguish them.
takeaway: A time embedding lets one set of weights handle many corruption levels.
explanation_steps: One set of weights handles every noise level.
(x_t,t)\longrightarrow\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)
Sin/cos time features → MLP → residual blocks.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: A batch can contain different timesteps
learning_goal: A batch can contain different timesteps
visual_description: A separate timestep and coefficient per example, reshaped for correct batched broadcasting.
narration: Each image may have a different timestep and independent Gaussian noise. Broadcasting must preserve each example coefficient. This displayed schedule is T=1000; the older experiment uses another T.
talk_through: Each image in this batch has its own time. Check that its coefficient broadcasts only across that image.
takeaway: The batch dimension binds each image to its own timestep and noise draw.
explanation_steps: t=[7,350,920]\in\mathbb Z^3
Gather three coefficients and reshape them to [3,1,1,1].
Input and target each have shape [3,1,28,28].
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Translate the picture into PyTorch
learning_goal: Translate the picture into PyTorch
visual_description: Annotated training update code; the right margin tracks data and control flow.
narration: The sentinel alpha_bar[0]=1 makes indices agree with mathematical time. Walk the active conceptual code line through the tuple diagram. Boilerplate and a readable named-layer model are in the executable companion.
talk_through: Match each line of code to the training example we just built: time, noise, input, prediction and loss.
takeaway: One training update needs one denoiser call on a batch of directly constructed noisy inputs.
explanation_steps: Sample a timestep and the target noise.
Gather each example’s coefficient and reshape it for broadcasting.
Use the forward formula to construct the noisy input.
Predict the noise, compute MSE and update the weights.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Where do the gradients go?
learning_goal: Where do the gradients go?
visual_description: Training branches: build the noisy input, predict its noise, and compare with the retained target. Gradients update the denoiser.
narration: The schedule and random draws are fixed within this gradient computation. We differentiate through the denoiser, not through an ancestral sampling chain. Sampling later keeps theta fixed.
talk_through: For this update, the sampled input and target are fixed. Which quantities can backpropagation change?
takeaway: Training updates the denoiser weights; it does not run the full generation chain.
explanation_steps: Backpropagation updates the denoiser parameters θ.
One training tuple needs a single denoiser call.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Where do the training labels come from?
learning_goal: Why this training needs no human noise labels
visual_description: Automatically constructed targets do not replace a representative clean dataset.
narration: A dataset containing only sevens can teach a seven-shaped prior but does not establish coverage of all digits. Self-generated noise labels remove one annotation need, not the need for representative data.
talk_through: Adding noise gives us labels for free. What would still be missing if the dataset contained only sevens?
takeaway: We can create noise targets automatically, but the clean dataset still determines what the model can learn.
explanation_steps: We create the noise labels when we corrupt the images.
We still need clean examples that represent the data we want to generate.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: The ELBO from Lecture I appears again
learning_goal: The ELBO from Lecture I appears again
visual_description: One latent path with forward and learned reverse arrows, grouped into the three bound contributions.
narration: Replace the VAE latent z by a whole latent path. q(x(t-1)|xt,x0) is tractable because training knows x0; q(x(t-1)|xt) integrates it out. The full equality, expectations and endpoint likelihood are in Appendices A2 and A3. The minus sign on log likelihood matters.
talk_through: Recall the VAE bound. Here the latent variable is a whole noisy path rather than one latent vector.
takeaway: The diffusion bound combines a prior term, local reverse-matching terms and an endpoint likelihood.
explanation_steps: \log p_\theta(x_0)\geq\operatorname{ELBO}(x_0)
q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_t q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})
p_\theta(x_{0:T})=p(x_T)\prod_t p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
Negative bound = prior KL + local KL terms − expected log likelihood.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: How does the bound lead to noise MSE?
learning_goal: Why did this become noise MSE?
visual_description: With fixed covariance, Gaussian KL depends quadratically on the difference of means.
narration: C is independent of the learned mean for fixed covariances. Substituting the epsilon mean gives the shown weight. Never evaluate that t>1 weight at t=1 where posterior variance is zero. Endpoints and likelihood discretisation are also not retained by simplified MSE.
talk_through: With fixed Gaussian variances, matching means becomes squared error. Substituting the noise prediction gives these weights.
takeaway: Simple noise MSE changes the variational weighting and does not include every term of the negative ELBO.
explanation_steps: \mathrm{KL}(\mathcal N(\tilde\mu_t,\tilde\beta_t I)\Vert\mathcal N(\mu_\theta,\sigma_t^2 I))=\frac{\|\tilde\mu_t-\mu_\theta\|^2}{2\sigma_t^2}+C
w_t=\frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)},\quad t>1

\mathcal L_{simple}=\mathbb E_{x_0,t,\epsilon}\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2

Simple MSE drops the time-dependent weights and the other bound terms.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Sampling starts without a clean image
learning_goal: Sampling starts without a clean image
visual_description: Sampling loop: random noise, shared denoiser, reverse transition, feedback of sampled state.
narration: The displayed image illustrates a noisy state. Actual model sampling uses a new Gaussian draw with no clean reference. Intermediate random draws and the initial state are separate sources of stochasticity.
talk_through: During training we started with a clean image. At generation time, we have only a fresh Gaussian draw.
takeaway: Generation keeps the learned weights fixed and repeatedly samples a less noisy state.
explanation_steps: x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I)
Keep θ fixed and repeatedly sample a previous state.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: A predicted clean image is useful
learning_goal: A predicted clean image is useful
visual_description: Worked inverse of the forward marginal: subtract estimated noise, then divide by the signal coefficient.
narration: First subtract estimated aggregate noise, then undo signal scaling. At large t, division by a very small coefficient amplifies prediction error. This is an estimated clean image; clipping a display does not validate it.
talk_through: Undo the forward formula: subtract the estimated noise contribution, then divide out the signal scaling.
takeaway: The predicted noise gives a clean-image estimate, though small signal coefficients can amplify its error.
explanation_steps: x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\hat\epsilon
\hat x_0=\frac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\hat\epsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}
\hat x_0=\frac{.5-.6(-.4)}{.8}=.925
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Which state goes into the next call?
learning_goal: Which value enters the next call?
visual_description: The noise prediction gives a clean estimate and a previous noisy state; only the previous state is fed back.
narration: Keep the three quantities in separate labelled panels. Estimating clean data is useful for parameterising a mean, but cannot silently replace the next sampled chain state.
question: Which value enters the next call?
answer: The sampled x(t-1).
talk_through: The clean estimate answers one question. The sampler needs a different quantity: the state at the previous time.
takeaway: The next denoiser call receives the sampled previous state, with the noise level expected at that time.
explanation_steps: The clean estimate asks what the original image might have been.
The next state still needs the noise level associated with t−1.
Pass the sampled x(t−1) to the next denoiser call.
visual_revision: Whole-deck scene review: source-aware figures, unique visible labels, retained presenter cue and takeaway.

title: Build one reverse transition
learning_goal: Parameterize one reverse distribution
visual_description: An internally consistent beta point two reverse-mean fixture; one-step alpha is used in the final division.
narration: This denominator is one-step alpha, not alpha-bar. The Gaussian parameterisation approximates the unknown reverse conditional; a coarse true reverse need not be Gaussian. Appendix A4 derives the tractable posterior and then substitutes the clean estimate.
talk_through: Use the noise prediction to set the centre of a Gaussian transition. Check which alpha appears in the denominator.
takeaway: The reverse mean uses one-step alpha; alpha-bar appears in the correction for predicted noise.
explanation_steps: p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(x_t,t),\sigma_t^2 I)
\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t),\quad c_t=\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}
x_t-c_t\hat\epsilon
\mu_\theta=\frac{x_t-c_t\hat\epsilon}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}

title: Why add noise during denoising?

question: A lower bound on log evidence
answer: Jensen applies because log is concave. The posterior KL gap is nonnegative. The exact expectation is a lower bound; a single Monte Carlo realisation need not be below the evidence. This connects to the VAE derivation.

\log p_\theta(x_0)=\mathrm{ELBO}+D_{KL}(q(x_{1:T}|x_0)\Vert p_\theta(x_{1:T}|x_0))

question: Masked language: objective and sampling convention
answer: Each modelled position is independently masked with probability t. The 1/t weight is required for this LLaDA-style objective. A simple unweighted masked-position cross-entropy is pedagogical but is not numerically the same objective. Other samplers use confidence-based remasking and different length handling.
talk_through: At time t, each response position is masked with probability t. The objective weights its masked-token loss by 1/t.
takeaway: The time weighting is part of this objective, so unweighted masked cross-entropy is a different loss.
explanation_steps: \mathcal L=-\mathbb E_{t,x_0,x_t}\left[\frac1t\sum_i\mathbf1[x_t^i=MASK]\log p_\theta(x_0^i|x_t)\right]
t is uniform on (0,1]; sum over modelled response positions. No sequence-length division here.
Our scripted sampler: three response slots, reveal one per step, observed prompt fixed, no remasking.
